content.summary_of_the_paper:
The main contribution of this paper is the introduction of a quadratic programming accuracy predictor based on the architecture parameter.
Such predictor enjoys a closed-form solution and is more sample-efficient than commonly used MLP-based predictor.
Combining the predictor and the latency constraint, the author also proposes an optimization method based on the Frank-Wolfe algorithm.
content.main_review:
**Strong Points**
- I like the idea of using simple quadratic formulation for the accuracy predictor, which is more concise and easy to interpret.
- It's good to present the insights for the architecture design from the learnt predictor like increasing the expansion ratio for deeper stages.

**Weak Points and Question**
- This paper resembles the HardCoRe-NAS [1] to a large extent, the writing for the introduction is identical, Figure 1 in this paper and Figure 2 in [1] are exactly the same. Theorem 3.3 and Theorem 3.1 in [1] are similar. Besides, [1] also introduces the quadratic programming formulation and they both use the block coordinate SFW to solve the optimization problem. Moreover, the performance of IQNAS proposed in this paper over HardCoRe-NAS is marginal and not consistent.

[1] Neyman et al. HardCoRe-NAS: Hard Constrained diffeRentiable Neural Architecture Search. 2021.

replying_to: Replying to Official Review of Paper1899 by Reviewer SHia

content.title: Author Response (1/2)
content.comment:
We thank the reviewer for acknowledging the concise and easy to interpret of the introduced quadratic formulation for the accuracy estimator and benefits of the derived insights for the architecture design.

Q) “This paper resembles the HardCoRe-NAS to a large extent, the writing for the introduction is identical, Figure 1 in this paper and Figure 2 in HardCoRe-NAS are exactly the same.”

A) Indeed, we adopted the first paragraphs of the introduction as the motivation for the constrained NAS problem is similar and was properly put by the authors of HardCoRe-NAS, from there on the path diverged. 
The search space we use is a MobileNetV2 based search space, the same as of HardCoRe-NAS, which is also very similar to the one of FB-Net, MNASNet, MobileNetV2, EfficientNet, TF-NAS, etc. This search space is the common choice for NAS of efficient models as stated in the main text. We never claim this part to be novel, but rather a technical section. We give a detailed description of this search space, with proper references, in order for the paper to be as self-contained as possible and for a proper introduction of the notations used throughout this paper. We added Figure 1 for the convenience of the reader, as we believe it is easier to understand the search space with visualizations. We gave proper citations throughout the paper and specifically the search space section and used the figure with the authors’ consent. 

Regardless, we removed this figure from the revision and rewrote this section and the similar parts of the introduction.

Q) “Theorem 3.3 and Theorem 3.1 in HardCore-NAS are similar.”

A) Although Theorem 3.3 and Theorem 3.1 in HardCore-NAS state the same sparsity result, those are proven for the solutions of different algorithms. While the latter is proven for a projection step which is not required by IQNAS, the former is proven for the output Algorithm 1: Block Coordinate Frank-Wolfe (BCFW) with Line Search for BLCP. Those are thus essentially different results while superficially have similar appearances. 

Q) “Besides, HardCore-NAS also introduces the quadratic programming formulation and they both use the block coordinate SFW to solve the optimization problem.”

A) Actually, HardCoRe-NAS does not introduce any quadratic programming formulation but only a quadratic form of the latency constraint, which is indeed utilized by this work and is not claimed to be novel anywhere in this paper. The optimization objective of HardCoRe-NAS is stochastic, certainly not quadratic and requires backpropagation through a supernetwork and hence uses the block coordinate Stocastic FW, that involves stochastic gradients and is not provided with theoretical guarantees and requires for several GPU hours. 
Hence it also requires access to a powerful GPU to perform the search (and not only the fine-tuning) and lacks interpretability.

This work however, formulates a simple deterministic quadratic objective function that together with the quadratic latency constraint form a quadratic programming problem. Along with two other out-of-the-box tools, a designated block coordinate FW (not stochastic) with line-search is introduced for solving the quadratic program in just several minutes over a common CPU along with convergence and sparsity guarantees. 

Moreover, recently [45] pointed out the inconsistencies associated with using gradient information as a proxy for the quality of the architectures, while HardCoRe-NAS relies heavily on such gradient information, our method does not use gradients at all for assessing the quality of design decisions and the method does not even have to be differentiable for all that matters.

The two formulations are thus fundamentally different.

replying_to: Replying to Official Review of Paper1899 by Reviewer B5Jb

content.title: Author Response
content.comment:
We thank the reviewer for acknowledging the interpretability of the quadratic form, the benefits over more complicated predictors and the insights derived from our formulation.

Q) “The predictor baselines compared are insufficient. There are more predictors other than MLP or Bilinear. More baselines in White (2021) are suggested.”

A) The purpose of this work is not to compare many accuracy predictors. White et al. (2021) have already done that comprehensively. In this work we introduce an interpretable bilinear accuracy estimator to formulate the NAS problem as an IQCQP with all the benefits that comes with that. Then each comparison to other predictors has its purpose:
- Comparing to a learned bilinear predictor shows that the efficient way we suggest to construct the estimator is more sample efficient than learning the parameters of the same functional form, e.g. by solving a linear regression problem.
- Comparing to a quadratic predictor shows that omitting the interactions between microscopic decisions (alpha parameters) to each other and of macroscopic decisions (beta parameters) to each other does not cause much degradation of the constructed bilinear accuracy estimator (and also of the learned bilinear version) compared to the quadratic predictor.
- Comparing to a MLP predictor shows that the simple bilinear parametric form does not lack the expressive power required for properly rank architectures’ accuracies. The MLP predictor is merely given as one commonly used example for such parameter heavy predictor (OFA, NSGANetV2, etc.). To support this point, we do not think other complex predictors should be given but a common one is sufficient.

Q) “The way to estimate the contribution of different terms of the accuracy estimator (4.2.1) seems unclear. A question for authors: How are the two variants implemented? By simply setting the coefficient in the optimized quadratic form to 0, or set them to 0 before optimized?”

A) Actually, there is no optimization happening whatsoever for constructing the accuracy estimator but the parameters of the estimator (equations 3 and 4) are empirically measured as described in section 3.2.1. Then groups of those parameters are set to zero instead of the values measured so we learn about the importance of those parameters.

Q) “Though interesting, the insights are not verified by further experiments. We cannot identify whether the insights are correct.”

A) Actually the logic is the other way around: since the accuracy estimator is shown to be reliable both theoretically (theorem 3.1) and empirically (Figures 2 - Right), the insights derived from it should be correct. Moreover, the design rules extracted from this estimator (Figure 6) are effectively those followed when setting this very estimator as an objective function for the NAS problem. Thus, indeed, following those design rules by optimizing this objective yields results that surpass or are comparable with other state-of-the-art NAS methods. This further supports the validity of the derived insights.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper proposed a method to estimate the accuracy and latency in NAS problem. Specifically, it uses a quadratic formulation for both accuracy and latency predictor, and shows that this simple form is accurate enough in predicting the accuracy of a trained weight-sharing super-network on ImageNet classification. Following the idea of super-network, the authors proposed a NAS framework which use weight-sharing to train a supernet, then use the proposed method to estimate a quadratic model of accuracy predictor and latency predictor.
content.main_review:
Strength:
The main contribution of this paper is proposing the quadratic accuracy predictor and showing such simple model could be accurate enough to reach the comparable NAS accuracy and correlation (Kendall-Tau). The significance of using quadratic estimation model is obvious: they are well studied problem and many tools can be used to get a reasonable good solution.

Weekness:
However, it's still not clear in the advantage of using such accuracy predictor. In Figure 2, the authors show that the correlation is high with this accuracy predictor, but it's not clear how those samples are generated and how is the sampling space, which are very important. For example, if different samples have distinct capacity differences, it's easy to get the predictor to predict the larger model to have better accuracy. However, in the NAS search, we want to know with the same model size/flops/latency, how is the accuracy's ranking. So it's better to show that given the similar latency, how is such rank correlation. In the experiments, to fully validate the effectiveness of the proposed accuracy predictor, I suggest the authors to apply the proposed predictor onto other NAS frameworks, instead of proposing another one, which makes the advantage of the accuracy predictor not clear. I would also recommended the authors to conduct experiment on other search space and tasks, to further validate the proposed accuracy predictor.

replying_to: Replying to Official Review of Paper1899 by Reviewer 82xa

content.title: Author Response
content.comment:
We thank the reviewer for acknowledging the “obvious significance” of our formulation and the method being simple and accurate.

Q) “it's still not clear in the advantage of using such accuracy predictor. In Figure 2, the authors show that the correlation is high with this accuracy predictor, but it's not clear how those samples are generated and how is the sampling space, which are very important.”

A) In section 4.1.1, the way those samples are generated are expressed: “The test set for evaluating the ranking correlations of all the accuracy predictors is composed of another 500 samples generated uniformly…” (at random from the search space). We argue that sampling sub-networks uniformly at random from the search space is the most unbiased and fair thing to do for evaluating the accuracy predictors. We made this standing out more clearly.

Q) “For example, if different samples have distinct capacity differences, it's easy to get the predictor to predict the larger model to have better accuracy.”

A) The search space is extremely fine grained in terms of accuracy differences of different samples, as can be seen in Figure 2 (Left) from the dense x-axis values of the 500 test samples picked uniformly at random from the search space. The search space includes a certain block of a certain stage being with kernel size 3x3 or 5x5 for example. The resulting difference in accuracy is a small fraction of percentage. Similar values for ranking correlation coefficients and MSE are obtained when sampling 10,000 sub-network at random. 

Q) “However, in the NAS search, we want to know with the same model size/flops/latency, how is the accuracy's ranking. So it's better to show that given the similar latency, how is such rank correlation.”

A) In NAS we effectively want to rank architecture regardless of their size/flops/latency, while usually those properties correlate with the accuracy. Specifically, the accuracy estimator ranks well architectures of close latencies. This is implicitly demonstrated by outperforming random search. Random search samples many architectures of the same latency for many latency values. Consistently outperforming random search, means that the ranking of architectures is performed well for every latency value such that a superior architecture is selected. Many methods, that we compare to, pick the best sample out of many samples of close latencies, e.g. Tan et al. (2019) (Figure 6). Outperforming all of those methods (Figure 5 and Table 1) implicitly shows that our method outperforms random search as well, while selecting better architectures for a certain latency than those randomly sampled for the same latency. Regardless we might add such explicit experiments in the revision.

Mingxing Tan, Bo Chen, Ruoming Pang, Vijay Vasudevan, Mark Sandler, Andrew Howard, and Quoc V Le. Mnasnet: Platform-aware neural architecture search for mobile. In Proceedings of the IEEE Conference on Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition, pp. 2820–2828, 2019.


Q) “In the experiments, to fully validate the effectiveness of the proposed accuracy predictor, I suggest the authors to apply the proposed predictor onto other NAS frameworks, instead of proposing another one, which makes the advantage of the accuracy predictor not clear.”

A) This comment is rather general. We simply sample 500 sub-network from the search space uniformly at random, measure their one-shot model’s accuracy and measure the ranking correlations with the accuracy predictions of the estimator. This is merely “proposing another one”. We respectfully argue that this is the most unbiased and fair test to perform. The accuracy estimator yields extremely high ranking correlation coefficients for this search space and once served as an objective function the method generates state-of-the-art architectures. Furthermore, it is interpretable and thus provide many insights and design rules for CNNs. We hence respectfully believe, that the advantage of the accuracy estimator is rather clear. 

Q) “I would also recommended the authors to conduct experiment on other search space and tasks, to further validate the proposed accuracy predictor.”
A) Both the novel accuracy estimator and the adapted latency constraint are constructed to express the accuracy and latency of sub-networks sampled from an Inverted Bottleneck (MobilenetV2) based search spaces. For example, DARTS search space has a completely different structure such that most methods applied on the former do not apply to the later and vice versa, including the only other interpretable framework we know of Ru et al. (2021).

Binxin Ru, Xingchen Wan, Xiaowen Dong, and Michael Osborne. Interpretable neural architecture search via bayesian optimisation with weisfeiler-lehman kernels. In International Conference on Learning Representations, 2021.

display_title: Official Review of Paper1899 by Reviewer 31pM

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper proposes IQNAS, a method for  constrained neural architecture search (NAS) demonstrated with the application of designing latency-constrained neural networks. The proposed method is intended to learn a simple and interpretible neural network performance predictor, used in combination  with  a scalable search method with theoretical guarantees. They achieve  this by proposing a quadratic accuracy estimator that measures the accuracy contribution of individual design choices and then maximizes this objective under quadratic latency constraints. The quadratic program  can be solved using an out-of-the-box Mixed Integer Quadratic Constraints Programming toolbox.  Experiments show that the method obtains some improvement in performance over existing methods, especially in terms of reducing the computational cost of search.
content.main_review:
Strengths:
1. The paper proposes a performance predictor for constrained NAS that can be solved as a quadratic program. This is the main advantage of the proposed method over existing work that uses parametric performance predictors  (e.g. neural nets). 
2. The interpretable nature of the quadratic program allows us to understand what design choices are important for creating a constrained architecture. 

Weaknesses/Questions
The search space and many design choices in the paper seem identical to HardCoRe-NAS (Nayman et al., 2021). While HardCoRe-NAS uses a different, differentiable method for optimization, the performance gain of IQNAS over  HardCoRe-NAS in terms of obtaining more accurate architectures  with same latency is very small (or in several cases HardCoRe-NAS outperforms IQNAS). The main advantages of IQNAS seem to be a reduction in search cost of about 50%. Can authors comment on the significant improvements in this work over HardCoRe-NAS?

Minor comment: Figure 1 in this paper is identical to Figure 2 from HardCoRe-NAS (Nayman et al., 2021). Please add a citation to that paper in the caption.

content.title: Author Response (2/2)
content.comment:
Q) “The paper proposes a more efficient to optimize method for constrained NAS and shows modest improvement over prior work using the same search space. I am not sure if the methodological improvement is enough to warrant a publication as an ICLR paper.”

A) Considering the results in the table above, we believe that the improvements are not modest as outperforming state-of-the-art results should not be taken for granted. Despite that, 50% reduction in the marginal search cost is not modest for real applications at scale. The methodological improvements include, but are not limited to, the interpretability of the NAS algorithm to quantify the contribution and importance of design choices in CNNs. This is the first work to introduce such property for this broadly used search space and the second for NAS in general. Hence, overall, we believe that we propose an interesting view of the problem, with some interesting insights and evident benefits for practical applications that have place as an ICLR publication.

content.title: Author Response (1/2)
content.comment:
We thank the reviewer for acknowledging some of the strengths of this work as “the interpretable nature of the quadratic program allows us to understand what design choices are important” and the simple accuracy estimator that allows that together with the formulation of a quadratic program. 
Indeed, the mentioned interpretability is unique and rare in the field of NAS, and more specifically for this MobileNetV2 based search space. There is only a single work. that we know of, to provide interpretability for DARTS based search space as mentioned in the related work section, and it is more complex and somehow less intuitive.

We want to stress out that the introduced performance estimator is not “solved as a quadratic program” but rather intuitively and efficiently constructed from a sequence of realizations of the super-network. The learned quadratic predictors are only given as a more expensive alternative of matching performance to show that one should not expect to yield a better predictor by learning its parameters rather than assigning them in the way we propose. We made this point clearer in the revision of the paper.

Q) “The search space and many design choices in the paper seem identical to HardCoRe-NAS (Nayman et al., 2021). While HardCoRe-NAS uses a different, differentiable method for optimization, the performance gain of IQNAS over HardCoRe-NAS in terms of obtaining more accurate architectures with same latency is very small (or in several cases HardCoRe-NAS outperforms IQNAS). The main advantages of IQNAS seem to be a reduction in search cost of about 50%. Can authors comment on the significant improvements in this work over HardCoRe-NAS?״

A) Indeed, the search space we use is a MobileNetV2 based search space, the same as of HardCoRe-NAS, which is also very similar to the one of FB-Net, MNASNet, MobileNetV2, OFA, EfficientNet, TF-NAS, etc. This search space is the common choice for NAS of efficient models as stated in the main text. We never claim this part to be novel, but rather a technical section. We give a detailed description of this search space, with proper references, in order for the paper to be as self-contained as possible and for a proper introduction of the notations used throughout this paper. Indeed, the novelty of our work includes the construction of an interpretable accuracy estimator and formulating the NAS problem as a quadratic program with efficient deterministic algorithms for solving it in just several minutes over a common CPU, with some convergence guarantees. Differently, from HardCoRe-NAS which searches by a stochastic backpropagation over a supernetwork for several GPU hours per network without provided guarantees. Hence it also requires access to a powerful GPU to perform the search (and not only the fine-tuning) and lacks interpretability. Moreover, recently [45] pointed out the inconsistencies associated with using gradient information as a proxy for the quality of the architectures, while HardCoRe-NAS relies heavily on such gradient information, our method does not use gradients at all for assessing the quality of design decisions and the method does not even have to be differentiable for all that matters.

In terms of outperforming the Imagenet Top-1 accuracy of HardCoRe-NAS and others, one can use those 50% savings in the search cost for a longer fine-tune to consistently outperform HardCoRe-NAS under the same marginal cost for each generated architecture (15N). We present here the table that compares our method with HardCore-NAS following the practical search and fine-tune procedures proposed by by both methods, i.e. initialized the weights from the supernetwork and fine-tune with KD from the largest subnetwork:

| Model | Latency [ms] | Imagenet Top-1 [%] | Marginal Search Cost [GPU hours] |
|---|---|---|---|
| HardCoRe A| 40 | 75.9 | 15 |
 | Ours 40ms  | 40 | 76.3 | 8 |
| Ours 40ms  | 40 | 76.6 | 15 |
|||||
| HardCoRe B| 44 | 76.6 | 15 |
| Ours 45ms  | 45 | 76.8| 8 |
| Ours 45ms  | 45 | 77.0| 15 |
|||||
| HardCoRe C| 50 | 77.0 | 15 |
| Ours 50ms  | 50 | 77.2 | 8 |
| Ours 50ms  | 50 | 77.6 | 15 |
|||||
| HardCoRe D| 55 | 77.4 | 15 |
| Ours 55ms  | 55 | 77.5 | 8 |
| Ours 55ms  | 55 | 77.8 | 15 |
|||||
| HardCoRe D| 61 | 78.1 | 15 |
| Ours 60ms  | 59 | 77.8 | 8 |
| Ours 60ms  | 59 | 78.0 | 15 |

Thus, for practical purposes, one can either choose to use our method for a comparable performance with a reduced cost or for a better performance with a comparable cost.
